power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: One hundred and twenty-four university students participated at Time 1. Ten did not complete the survey and 16 failed the manipulation check, leaving 98 participants (20 men, 76 women, 2 other; Mage = 19.55, SD = 1.42). Fifty-five completed Time 2foot_0 . G*Power 3.1.9.6 (Faul et al., 2007) indicated that N = 55 provided 80% power to detect a medium effect (f² = .15) in a onepredictor linear regression at α = .05. The study received university research ethics approval; participants provided informed consent and received course credit.

An a priori G*Power 3.1.9.7 analysis based on the effects in Studies 1 and 2 indicated that 101 participants per condition were required to detect f² = .08 with 80% power at α = .05. Allowing 10% attrition produced a target of 111 per condition (N = 333), which was achieved. The study received university research ethics approval; participants provided informed consent and received £2.50.

You reported a power analysis that has been classified as 'post-hoc'. Calculating observed power is [almost never useful](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/08-samplesizejustification.html#sec-posthocpower). If you actually performed a sensitivity power analysis, label it as such explicitly.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Conditions and mechanisms of Human-AI synergy in everyday decision making
table.research_questions:
H1: The fully AI-augmented MAU will more accurately predict satisfaction with decision outcome at Time 1 and Time 2 than the human-only MAU or AI-only ratings.
H2: Participants in the fully AI-augmented MAU condition will select more attributes than in the human-only MAU condition.
table.foreknowledge_of_data_or_evidence: Data does not yet exist. No part of the data that will be used for this analysis plan exists, and no part will be generated until after this plan is registered.
table.study_type: Randomized Experiment: Must include random assignment of subjects to treatments or conditions. This usually includes lab experiments, field experiments, intervention experiments, randomized controlled trials, and A/B testing.
table.study_design_overview: The study will use a mixed design with condition as the between-subjects factor and time as the within-subjects factor. Participants will be randomly assigned to one of three between-subjects conditions: AI-only, human-only MAU, or fully AI-augmented MAU. The within-subjects factor will be time, with outcomes assessed at two time points: Time 1, corresponding to the initial decision, and Time 2, corresponding to the follow-up assessment.
table.randomization: We will use simple randomisation, conducted through the software Qualtrics, to randomly allocate participants into one of three conditions.
table.data_collection_procedures: The study will recruit participants via Prolific Academic (prolific.co). Participants will be adults over 18 years of age, with a UK birthplace, and English as their first language. They will be invited to participate in a two part study about everyday decision making. Part 1 will be 25 minutes long with a £2.50 participation fee. Part 2 will be 5 minutes long with a £0.50 participation fee.
table.sample_size: A total of 333 participants will be recruited, with 111 participants in each experimental condition.
table.sample_size_rationale: A power analysis was conducted using G*Power version 3.1.9.7 (Faul et al., 2007). Based on a small to medium effect size, f2 = 0.08 (Cohen, 1988) with a significance criterion of α = .05 and power = 0.80, the minimum sample size required for this effect in a linear regression is N = 101. A further 10% was included to allow for attrition at Time 2, resulting in a total sample size of N = 111 per condition at Time 1. This is required for all three conditions in the between subjects design, resulting in a total of 333 participants.
table.stopping_rule: Data collection will terminate once our target sample size of useable data (following pre-defined exclusion criteria) is met.
table.manipulated_variables:
The manipulated variable will be the level of decision analysis. There will be three conditions:

1.	In the AI-only condition, the decision and both options under consideration will be passed to the OpenAI API via the Qualtrics Webservice, where they will be processed using the GPT-5.4 model with a temperature of 0.7. A separate prompt will be sent to elicit an evaluation of each decision option in turn.
The prompt will be:
“How good or bad would the outcome of the choice of [first option they report] be when deciding about [the decision they report]? Base your response on the typical opinion of the general public. Respond using one of the following options: extremely bad outcome, moderately bad outcome, slightly bad outcome, neither good nor bad outcome, slightly good outcome, moderately good outcome, extremely good outcome.”
This will be repeated to obtain a rating for the second option reported. Participants will not be told the AI response.

2.	In the human-only MAU condition, participants will complete a multi-attribute utility evaluation for each option. First, participants will generate a set of decision-relevant factors (attributes) that they consider important for evaluating the options. Next, they will assign a relative importance weight to each attribute, such that higher values will reflect greater perceived importance. Participants will then evaluate each option by providing a rating of its expected outcome on each factor. Specifically, they will report up to six attributes that they consider important when making this decision. They will rate how important each attribute is on a scale from 0, not at all important, to 5, extremely important. Then, for each attribute, they will rate each option separately on a scale from -3 to +3, where -3 will indicate an extremely negative outcome and +3 will indicate an extremely positive outcome.
For each option, an overall evaluation score will be computed as the weighted sum of its attribute ratings. Each attribute rating will be multiplied by its corresponding weight, and these products will be summed across all attributes to yield a single composite score for that option. Higher scores will indicate more favourable overall evaluations. This score will not be shown to participants.

3.	In the fully AI-augmented MAU condition, participants will complete the same multi-attribute utility evaluation. In addition, their decision and two options will be passed to GPT-5.4 via the OpenAI API to mirror each step of the process by: a) generating six attributes relevant to the decision, b) rating the importance of each attribute, and c) rating the expected outcome on each attribute for each option. A temperature of 0.7 will be used. The prompts for each of these will be:
“List one factor that you should consider when deciding about [the decision they reported]. The choice is between [first option reported] and [second option reported].”
This prompt will be repeated six times, with previous responses included and with instructions to prevent repetition.
“How important is the factor [each factor is included in turn] when deciding about [the decision they reported]? Base your response on the typical opinion of the general public. Respond using one of the following options: 0 Not at all important, 1 Slightly important, 2 Somewhat important, 3 Moderately important, 4 Very important, 5 Extremely important. Write one brief sentence justifying your response.”
Participants will then be presented with a combined list of all the attributes they generated and those generated by AI. They will be instructed to choose the most relevant attributes for their decision, which may include any combination of self-generated and AI-generated attributes. Participants will be presented with their initial rating of the value of each attribute for each option, alongside the AI’s rating and its one-sentence justification. They will be asked to consider both of these and then provide their final rating. Final ratings will be used to calculate the multi-attribute utility of each option as the weighted sum of its attribute ratings, as in the human-only MAU condition. This score will not be shown to participants.
table.measured_variables:
Decision outcome will be assessed with the five item Satisfaction with Decision Outcome scale. The tense of the items will be adjusted for Time 1 and Time 2. Participants will respond on a 5-point Likert scale (1 = “strongly disagree” to 5 = “strongly agree”).

Satisfaction With Decision Outcome (Time 1)

1.	The outcome of the decision I made will turn out well overall.
2.	The benefits of the decision I made will outweigh the costs.
3.	The outcome will match or exceed what I am trying to achieve.
4.	The outcome will be better than the realistic alternatives I could choose.
5.	Overall, the outcome of my decision will be successful.

Satisfaction With Decision Outcome (Time 2)
1.	The outcome of the decision I made turned out well overall.
2.	The benefits of the decision I made have outweighed the costs.
3.	The outcome has matched or exceeded what I was trying to achieve when I made the decision.
4.	The outcome was better than the realistic alternatives I could have chosen.
5.	Overall, the outcome of my decision was successful.
table.indices: The Satisfaction with Decision Outcome score will be calculated as the mean of the items in the scale.
table.statistical_tests:
For Hypothesis 1, linear regression will be used to assess how well the rating of the chosen option from each condition predicts the satisfaction with decision outcome at Time 1 and Time 2.

For hypothesis 2, a t test will be used to test for differences in the number of attributes selected for the final rating in the fully AI-augmented MAU condition than the human-only MAU condition.
table.inference_criteria:
All statistical analyses will be conducted using a significance threshold of α = .05.
For hypothesis 1, regression models will be compared across conditions using common AIC conventions. ΔAIC ≤ 2 indicates models are essentially indistinguishable, ΔAIC = 4–7 indicate clear support for the lower AIC model over its competitor, and ΔAIC > 10 indicates substantial support for the lower AIC model (Burnham & Anderson, 2004).
table.data_exclusion_criteria:
Cases will be excluded from the final sample based on the following criteria: 

1. Incomplete data
2. Failing the attention check
3. ReCAPTCHA score < 0.3
4. Not reporting an appropriate decision
5. Failure of the model to return output
table.missing_data_handling: Responses with any missing data will be excluded from analyses.

table.indices: The Satisfaction with Decision Outcome score will be calculated as the mean of the items in the scale.
table.statistical_tests:
For Hypothesis 1, linear regression will be used to assess how well the rating of the chosen option from each condition predicts the satisfaction with decision outcome at Time 1 and Time 2.

For hypothesis 2, a t test will be used to test for differences in the number of attributes selected for the final rating in the fully AI-augmented MAU condition than the human-only MAU condition.
table.inference_criteria:
All statistical analyses will be conducted using a significance threshold of α = .05.
For hypothesis 1, regression models will be compared across conditions using common AIC conventions. ΔAIC ≤ 2 indicates models are essentially indistinguishable, ΔAIC = 4–7 indicate clear support for the lower AIC model over its competitor, and ΔAIC > 10 indicates substantial support for the lower AIC model (Burnham & Anderson, 2004).
table.data_exclusion_criteria:
Cases will be excluded from the final sample based on the following criteria: 

1. Incomplete data
2. Failing the attention check
3. ReCAPTCHA score < 0.3
4. Not reporting an appropriate decision
5. Failure of the model to return output
table.missing_data_handling: Responses with any missing data will be excluded from analyses.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. :::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 771 columns across 6 data files.
#### Issues Identified

713 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.
#### Careless Responding

18 distinct respondents were flagged for **straightlining**: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is **one row per person**, and the *Longest run* column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.

Of these, **18 were flagged *only* by short-scale straightlining** (a run of identical answers on a scale of 7 items or fewer). On a short, one-directional scale, answering consistently is often normal, coherent responding rather than carelessness — treat these as weak signals and inspect the actual responses before excluding anyone.
These are prompts to inspect those rows, not definitive judgements.

**What this does not cover.** Only 1 of 6 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

text.text: Artificial intelligence (AI) can improve human judgement, but human-AI systems rarely achieve complementarity: combined performance exceeding that of both humans and AI alone.

Across three longitudinal studies (N = 671), we tested whether large language models (LLMs) could support complementarity by contributing to the construction and revision of everyday decision representations.
Participants reported real, personally meaningful decisions involving two options and the decision outcome success one week later.
As decisions were participant-generated rather than predefined, LLMs dynamically generated considerations and alternative evaluations tailored to each decision.
We compared the predictive validity of AI, Human, and augmented evaluations.
AI evaluations were standalone LLM predictions of decision outcome success.
Human weightedadditive evaluations combined participant-generated attributes, importance weights, and option ratings.
Augmented evaluations incorporated LLM-generated attributes and, in later studies, suggested weights and ratings, while participants selected attributes and retained control over evaluations.
Augmented evaluations consistently predicted experienced outcomes and showed the strongest observed associations across all three studies.

Evidence for complementarity was clearest in Study 2, where fully augmented evaluations outperformed both standalone approaches and explained additional variance in expected and experienced outcomes beyond the standalone evaluations considered together.
Across studies, augmentation expanded the attribute set, with participants retaining human and AI contributions.
These findings show that human-AI complementarity can emerge in predicting success of real decision outcomes and suggest that decision architecture matters.

A distributed cognitive system that integrates AI contributions across all stages of decision making while humans remain responsible for selection and judgement of personally relevant considerations offers a promising architecture for evaluating diverse, personally meaningful real-life decisions.
found that prompting LLMs to explore alternative solutions produced ideas rated more highly than those of human groups, although human ideas were more novel.
These findings illustrate how differences in human and AI contributions may create complementary potential, although neither study directly demonstrated performance exceeding both standalone agents.
This potential does not automatically improve performance.
LLM outputs may be irrelevant, inaccurate, or biased (Echterhoff et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025), and access to a capable LLM does not ensure that its information will be used effectively.

text.text: Providing physicians with an LLM did not improve diagnostic reasoning in Goh et al. (2024), while Bean et al. (2026) found that participants given access to highly accurate LLMs performed no better than unaided participants.

(2026)</ref> found that participants given access to highly accurate LLMs performed no better than unaided participants.

text.text: Human-AI performance can therefore fall short of standalone AI when the surrounding interaction fails to elicit, interpret, or integrate its contributions effectively.

The real-world impact of an LLM depends not simply on what it can achieve independently, but how its capabilities can be incorporated into a decision process that complements human information and judgement (Sokol et al., 2025).
text.formatted: The real-world impact of an LLM depends not simply on what it can achieve independently, but how its capabilities can be incorporated into a decision process that complements human information and judgement <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Sokol et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Human-AI decision research commonly treats AI as an independent advisor whose recommendation the human may accept or revise (Bonaccio & Dalal, 2006; Lai et al., 2023; Vaccaro et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Human-AI decision research commonly treats AI as an independent advisor whose recommendation the human may accept or revise <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bonaccio & Dalal, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Lai et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Vaccaro et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Within this judge-advisor framework, performance depends largely on the quality of the AI's advice and whether the human relies on it appropriately (Lee & See, 2004; Schemmer et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Within this judge-advisor framework, performance depends largely on the quality of the AI's advice and whether the human relies on it appropriately <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Lee & See, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Schemmer et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Distributed cognition instead treats humans, technologies, and external representations as components of a single system that collectively processes information (Hutchins, 1995).
text.formatted: Distributed cognition instead treats humans, technologies, and external representations as components of a single system that collectively processes information <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Hutchins, 1995)</ref>.

text.text: This reframes understanding of the decision process from whether humans accept AI advice to how cognitive processes are allocated and coordinated across the system.
Research on groups similarly demonstrates the value of analysing the information processing of the system rather than its components in isolation (Banks & Millward, 2000; Hinsz et al., 1997).
text.formatted: Research on groups similarly demonstrates the value of analysing the information processing of the system rather than its components in isolation <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Banks & Millward, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Hinsz et al., 1997)</ref>.

text.text: Applied to human-AI decision making, the key question is whether cognitive work can be distributed so that the combined system exceeds either component working independently.
Everyday decisions often require alternatives to be compared across multiple factors (or attributes) whose costs and benefits must be traded off.
For example, we may need to choose between a job offer that is well paid but has an unpleasant commute or a less well paid job that is closer to home.
Multi-attribute utility theory provides a normative framework for such decisions (Keeney & Raiffa, 1976).
text.formatted: Multi-attribute utility theory provides a normative framework for such decisions <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Keeney & Raiffa, 1976)</ref>.

text.text: In practice, weighted-additive models approximate this logic by combining ratings of how well each option performs on relevant attributes with weights reflecting their importance (Payne et al., 1993).
text.formatted: In practice, weighted-additive models approximate this logic by combining ratings of how well each option performs on relevant attributes with weights reflecting their importance <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Payne et al., 1993)</ref>.

text.text: For preference-dependent decisions, these trade-offs depend on the individual's aims and circumstances, so there is no single objectively correct evaluation.
Constructing a comprehensive evaluation nevertheless requires relevant attributes to be identified, weighted, and used to assess each option.

Bounded cognitive capacity makes this difficult for unaided decision makers, who may construct incomplete representations of complex decisions because their cognitive limits mean that a full analysis of real-world decisions is intractable (Simon, 1955).
text.formatted: Bounded cognitive capacity makes this difficult for unaided decision makers, who may construct incomplete representations of complex decisions because their cognitive limits mean that a full analysis of real-world decisions is intractable <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Simon, 1955)</ref>.

text.text: We propose that LLMs can augment these components by generating additional considerations and alternative evaluations, while humans retain responsibility for judging their personal relevance.
Distributing these processes across human and AI may produce evaluations with greater predictive validity for experienced decision outcomes than either human or AI evaluations alone.
Everyday decisions provide a useful setting for studying real-world decision making.
They are personally meaningful, uncertain, and multi-attribute, but their outcomes can often be experienced within a relatively short period, providing a measure of decision success.

Unlike hypothetical tasks whose alternatives and relevant information are specified by the researcher, participant-generated decisions require an appropriate representation to be constructed for each individual.
This creates scope for LLMs to contribute additional considerations and alternative perspectives.
We use the naturalistic everyday decision-making task developed by Banks and Gamblin (2022).
text.formatted: We use the naturalistic everyday decision-making task developed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Banks and Gamblin (2022)</ref>.

text.text: Participants report a low-stakes, personally meaningful decision they are currently facing and identify two options.
They evaluate these two options.
One week later, they report their chosen option and experienced decision outcome.
For preference-dependent decisions without an objectively correct answer, a useful initial evaluation should capture how the decision maker subsequently experiences the chosen option.

We therefore assess evaluation quality through its prospective validity for reported outcomes, both their expectations of decision outcome success when the decision is made and their perceptions of decision outcome success when the outcome of the decision has been experienced.

Study 1 tests whether AI-generated attributes expand the considerations incorporated into participants' evaluations and whether combining AI breadth with human selection for personal relevance improves predictive validity.
Study 2 extends AI involvement to alternative importance weights and option ratings, allowing full augmentation to be compared with augmentation restricted to attribute generation.
It also explores whether greater divergence between human and AI evaluations is associated with greater augmentation benefit.
Study 3 independently compares AI, Human, and fully augmented evaluations in a between-participants design using a multi-item measure of perceived decision outcome success.
Across the studies, we predict that augmented evaluations will show greater predictive validity for experienced outcomes than Human or AI evaluations, indicating complementarity.

We also predict that full augmentation will outperform attribute augmentation alone in Study 2, and that augmentation will increase the number of attributes incorporated into evaluations across all three studies.
Study 1 used the everyday decision-making task developed by Banks and Gamblin (2022).
text.formatted: Study 1 used the everyday decision-making task developed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Banks and Gamblin (2022)</ref>.

text.text: Participants described a personally meaningful decision they were currently facing, identified two options, evaluated these options, and reported their chosen option.
One week later, they rated their experienced decision outcome success.
We compared three initial evaluations of each decision.
The AI evaluation was GPT-3.5's rating of each option.
The Human evaluation was a weightedadditive evaluation based on participant-generated attributes, importance weights, and option ratings.
For the augmented evaluation, the LLM generated six additional attributes.
Participants selected the most relevant attributes from the combined human-AI pool, and their ratings of the selected attributes were used to calculate an augmented weighted-additive evaluation.
The augmented procedure was designed to combine differing human and AI contributions.

The LLM could broaden the decision representation by identifying considerations that the participant had not spontaneously generated, but lacked access to the participant's preferences and circumstances.
Conversely, participants possessed this personal knowledge but might construct a relatively limited representation of the decision because of bounded cognitive capacity.
Participants therefore used their personal knowledge to select relevant considerations from the expanded information pool.

We predict that combining AI-generated breadth with human selection for personal relevance would produce an augmented evaluation with greater predictive validity for subsequently experienced decision success than either the Human or AI evaluation.

Participants reported a low-stakes everyday decision they were considering but had not yet made and described two options that they were evaluating.
They were instructed to exclude sensitive, distressing, or high-stakes decisions.
They reported their age and gender.
Participants next generated their own decision-relevant attributes.

They generated up to six relevant attributes, rated each attribute's importance from 0 (not at all important) to 5 (extremely important), and rated its expected effect on each option from -3 (extremely negative) to +3 (extremely positive).
They then rated six AI-generated attributes using the same scales, after completing the human-generated attributes.
Participants selected relevant attributes from the combined human-AI pool.
Where attributes were identified as duplicates, only the selected instance was retained.
Attributes were not re-rated; evaluation scores used the ratings already provided for the retained attributes.
Finally, participants indicated their intended option and rated "The decision will be successful" from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).

on a 7-point scale from extremely bad outcome to extremely good outcome.
Responses were checked against the Time 1 alternatives; participants who had not decided or selected another option were excluded.
Participants also rated satisfaction with their decision.
The present analyses focus on outcome success because the option evaluations concern anticipated outcomes, making experienced outcome success the theoretically matched criterion.
Analyses of satisfaction are presented in the supplementary materials.

For each option, the LLM rated how good or bad its outcome would be, based on the typical opinion of the general public.
Responses were restricted to seven verbal categories and coded from -3 (extremely bad) to +3 (extremely good), yielding one AI score per option.
The model was prompted six times to generate a factor relevant to the participant's decision, with previous responses included to prevent repetition, yielding six distinct attributes.
Human and Augmented scores.
Both were computed using a weighted-additive multi-attribute evaluation approach.

The Human score included participants' own attributes; the Augmented score included attributes retained from the combined pool.
Analysis Plan At Time 1, analyses used the evaluation score for the intended option; at Time 2, they used the Time 1 evaluation score for the option subsequently chosen.
At each time point, separate simple linear regressions tested the chosen option's AI, Human, and Augmented scores as predictors of decision success.
All simple linear regressions were estimated using 5,000 bootstrap samples.

Consistent with the human-AI complementarity literature (e.g. Bansal et al., 2021; Donahue, et al., 2022; Vaccaro et al., 2024) complementarity was operationalised as greater predictive validity for the augmented evaluation than for both standalone evaluations.

Thus, augmentation broadened the decision representation, with participants selectively retaining attributes from both sources.

At Time 1, all three evaluations predicted expected decision outcome success, but the Augmented model received substantially greater support than the Human and AI models, providing evidence of complementarity.
At Time 2, the Human and Augmented evaluations predicted experienced decision outcome success, whereas the AI evaluation did not.
Although the Augmented model again received the strongest support, it could not be reliably distinguished from the Human model.
Thus, evidence for complementarity was clear for immediate expectations but inconclusive for subsequently experienced outcomes.
Augmentation also expanded the decision representation.
Participants incorporated more attributes into the augmented evaluation than they had generated unaided and retained attributes from both human and AI sources.
Although they selected more AI-generated attributes in absolute terms, the proportions retained from each available set did not differ significantly.
Participants therefore appeared to filter the expanded information pool rather than simply adopt AI-generated information.
This pattern supports the proposed combination of AI breadth and human selection for personal relevance.
The Human model also received greater support than the AI model, highlighting the value of participants' access to their own preferences and circumstances.
Overall, Study 1 shows that incorporating AI-generated attributes can broaden decision representations and improve predictive validity.
However, attribute augmentation alone did not conclusively outperform human evaluation for experienced outcomes.
Study 2 therefore tests whether extending AI involvement to attribute weighting and option rating produces stronger evidence of complementarity.
Study 1 provided initial evidence for human-AI complementarity and showed that augmentation expanded the attributes incorporated into participants' evaluations.
However, evidence that the augmented evaluation exceeded the Human evaluation was stronger for expected decision success at Time 1 than for experienced decision success at Time 2.
Study 2 therefore increased the extent of augmentation and further examined how complementarity might arise.
First, we introduced a fully augmented weighted-additive evaluation.
In addition to generating attributes, the LLM proposed alternative importance weights and option ratings for participants to consider before making their final evaluations.
We compared this with the Human evaluation and the attribute-augmented evaluation used in Study 1.
We also constructed an AI weighted-additive evaluation (AI-WADD), in which the LLM generated the attributes, weights, and option ratings.
This provided a more structurally comparable AI benchmark alongside the direct AI rating.

We tested whether augmented evaluations, particularly full augmentation, showed greater predictive validity than the Human and AI evaluations, and whether full augmentation outperformed augmentation restricted to attribute generation.
We also examined whether fully augmented evaluations contributed predictive information about expected and experienced decision outcome success beyond Human and AI evaluations considered together.
Second, we explored whether greater disagreement between the human and AI-WADD evaluations was associated with a larger predictive advantage for full augmentation over Human evaluation.
Third, we tested whether augmentation again increased the number of attributes incorporated into evaluations and whether participants retained attributes from both human and AI sources.
Study 2 also used a larger online sample and replaced GPT-3.5 with GPT-4.5-preview.

At Time 1, the Human evaluation received the strongest support, followed by the Fully Augmented and Attribute-Augmented evaluations.
At Time 2, this ordering changed.
The Fully Augmented evaluation received the strongest support, followed by the Attribute-Augmented and Human evaluations.
Both augmented evaluations received greater support than the Human and AI evaluations, providing evidence of complementarity for experienced decision outcomes.
Full augmentation also substantially outperformed attribute augmentation alone, suggesting that AI contributions across multiple evaluation components produced additional benefit.
Fully augmented evaluations also explained additional variance in both expected and experienced decision outcome success beyond human evaluations and both AI evaluations considered together.
Thus, full augmentation contributed predictive information at both time points that was not fully captured by a linear combination of the standalone scores.
This is consistent with the potential value of constructing and revising evaluations through human-AI interaction.
These findings strengthen the evidence that human-AI complementarity can emerge in predicting experienced outcomes.
Unlike Study 1, where the Time 2 advantage over human evaluation was inconclusive, Study 2 provided clear evidence favouring both augmented evaluations.
As predicted by the distributed cognition account, the complementary advantage of full augmentation lies in how cognitive work is allocated across human and AI components.
However, augmentation did not outperform human evaluation for immediate expectations, indicating that its advantage was specific to predicting later experienced outcomes.
Study 2 also replicated representation expansion.

Participants incorporated more attributes into augmented evaluations than they generated unaided and retained similar numbers from human and AI sources, although they retained a greater proportion of their own attributes.
Thus, they drew on both sources while filtering information for personal relevance.
Finally, greater human-AI disagreement was associated with a larger predictive advantage for full augmentation over human evaluation.
This is consistent with the possibility that divergent information or perspectives create greater scope for augmentation to improve an evaluation.
Studies 1 and 2 provided initial evidence that augmentation can improve the predictive validity of weighted-additive evaluations of everyday decisions.
Augmentation expanded the attributes incorporated into participants' evaluations, while Study 2 showed that AI could also contribute alternative importance weights and option ratings.

The clearest evidence of complementarity emerged at Time 2 in Study 2, where the fully augmented evaluation showed greater predictive validity for experienced decision success than the Human and AI evaluations.
Both studies used within-participant designs, allowing alternative evaluations of the same decision to be compared.
However, participants reported decision outcomes after encountering AIgenerated attributes and evaluations, which may have influenced their judgements.
Study 3 therefore used a between-participants design in which participants were randomly assigned to an AI, Human, or fully augmented condition.
This allowed the predictive validity of independently obtained human, AI, and human-AI evaluations to be compared.
Study 3 also replaced the single-item decision outcome success measure with a five-item Perceived Decision Outcome Success Scale (PDOSS).
The measure assessed whether participants experienced the outcome as successful, beneficial, and consistent with their goals.

This provides broader and more reliable coverage of experienced outcomes, which is particularly important for preference-dependent decisions where whether an outcome is perceived as a success depends on the decision maker's personal aims, circumstances, and values.

We predict that the fully augmented evaluation would show greater predictive validity for subsequently experienced outcome success than either the Human or AI evaluation, providing evidence of complementarity.
We also predicted that participants in the fully augmented condition would incorporate more attributes into their evaluations than participants in the Human condition.

Study 3 compared independently obtained AI, Human, and Fully Augmented evaluations using a multi-item measure of perceived decision outcome success.
Fully Augmented evaluations showed the greatest descriptive predictive validity at both time points.
At Time 2, they explained 20% of the variance in experienced decision outcome success, compared with 16% for AI and 8% for Human evaluations.
This ordering was consistent with the pattern observed for experienced outcomes in Studies 1 and 2.
However, evaluation-by-condition interactions did not improve model fit, and Bayesian comparisons favoured a common-slope model at both time points.
Thus, although Fully Augmented evaluations showed the strongest descriptive associations, Study 3 did not independently establish that their predictive validity exceeded both standalone evaluations.
AI evaluations also predicted expected and experienced decision success and were descriptively stronger than Human evaluations.
This may partly reflect the more advanced LLM used in Study 3, or the fact that the pre-registered study was not adequately powered to test this exploratory analysis.
Study 3 also replicated representation expansion.

Fully Augmented evaluations incorporated more attributes than Human evaluations and drew on similar numbers of human-and AI-generated attributes, although selection was influenced by presentation order.
Augmentation therefore broadened the decision representation while preserving human selection of personally relevant information.
Across three longitudinal studies, we tested whether LLMs could support human-AI complementarity by contributing to evaluations of real, personally meaningful decisions.
As participants generated their own decisions, relevant representations had to be constructed dynamically for each individual.
LLMs contributed additional considerations and alternative perspectives that expanded the information represented.

Participants reported decisions they were currently facing and their experienced outcomes one week later, allowing us to compare the prospective validity of AI, Human, and augmented weighted-additive evaluations.
Four main findings emerged.
First, augmented evaluations were the strongest observed predictors of experienced decision outcome success across all three studies.
Evidence for complementarity was clearest in Study 2, where the Fully Augmented evaluation received substantially greater support than both standalone evaluations.
Fully augmented evaluations also explained additional variance beyond the standalone evaluations considered together, for both expected and experienced outcomes.
In Study 1, the Augmented evaluation was better supported than AI but not clearly better supported than Human evaluation.
In Study 3, it was descriptively strongest, but predictive slopes did not differ significantly between conditions.
Second, in Study 2, predictive validity was greater when AI contributed across multiple evaluation components than when it contributed only attributes.
Third, augmentation expanded the attribute set in every study, with participants retaining both self-generated and AI-generated attributes.
Fourth, greater human-AI disagreement was associated with a larger augmentation advantage over Human evaluation.
Findings for expected decision outcome success at Time 1 were less consistent.
As our primary question concerned prospective rather than concurrent validity, we focus on experienced outcomes reported at Time 2.
Human-AI complementarity remains difficult to achieve (Vaccaro et al., 2024), partly because many systems concentrate interaction around an AI recommendation that the human accepts or rejects.

The present studies tested such an architecture in open-ended, preference-dependent decisions.

In Study 2, fully augmented evaluations received more than ten times as much support as attribute augmentation alone when predicting experienced outcomes.

Hierarchical regressions further showed that fully augmented evaluations explained additional variance in both expected and experienced decision outcome success beyond human evaluations and both AI evaluations considered together.
This distinguishes two benefits of augmentation: stronger standalone prediction of experienced outcomes and additional predictive information at both time points.

A strength of these studies is their examination of genuine choices with experienced consequences.
However, only the chosen outcome could be experienced.
The findings therefore establish the prospective validity of evaluations for decision outcome success with the chosen outcome, not whether that option was better than the rejected alternative.
Predicting experienced outcomes remains valuable for choice, but future research designs that enable outcome information to be gathered for both options would be informative.

Following Banks and Gamblin (2022), outcomes were assessed after one week to accommodate most everyday decisions, although shorter decisions may have imposed greater recall demands.

text.text: The within-participant designs of Studies 1 and 2 and random allocation in Study 3 reduce the likelihood that this variability systematically favoured one evaluation approach.
Nevertheless, future studies could constrain decision timescales or tailor follow-up intervals to individual decisions.
Participants could generate a maximum of six attributes.
They did not, on average, retain all self-generated attributes in their augmented evaluations, suggesting that the cap did not routinely exclude essential considerations.
Nonetheless future research could use open-ended attribute elicitation.
Experienced perceptions of decision outcome success are necessarily subjective and may be influenced by post-decision processes such as dissonance reduction (Brehm, 1956).

text.text: However, for preference-dependent decisions, subjective experience is the outcome of interest rather than an imperfect substitute for an objective criterion.
Future research that combines experienced decision outcome success with behavioural or objective outcomes would provide an informative addition.
Nonetheless, it is central to the paradigm used here that a decision outcome perceived as a success by an individual, according to their personal preferences, is a meaningful assessment.
The process of constructing an evaluation of the decision could influence the features attended to in the subsequent rating.
It is therefore possible that AI-generated information influenced how participants came to judge their decisions rather than improving the prediction of their experience.
However, participants never saw the evaluation scores, so their later ratings could not be anchored on them.
Also, the outcome occurred a week later and concerned what happened, not the earlier evaluation.
Therefore it is unlikely that the association between evaluation and outcome rating is solely due to this effect.
Finally, the AI was prompted to adopt the typical opinion of the general public to provide a consistent reference point.
This may be less useful for people with unconventional preferences.

Personalised models could generate more individually relevant information, although our findings do indicate that greater human-AI agreement may also reduce access to genuinely different perspectives.

The association between disagreement and augmentation benefit suggests value in testing systems designed to introduce unshared information or devil's advocacy, drawing on hidden-profile research (Schulz-Hardt & Mojzisch, 2012; Leung & Urminsky, 2025).

text.text: Human-AI complementarity is rare in decision making.

Across three longitudinal studies, LLMaugmented evaluations consistently predicted perceived decision outcome success experienced one week later and showed stronger observed associations than human or AI evaluations.
Evidence for complementarity was clearest when AI contributed across multiple evaluation stages.
Augmentation broadened the decision representation, while humans selected personally relevant information and retained control over final judgements.
These findings show how complementarity can emerge from a distributed cognitive architecture that allocates different forms of cognitive work across humans and AI.
Integrating AI contributions throughout evaluation while preserving human judgement offers a promising approach to evaluating real-life decisions.
